  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.

  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);

    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.

      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Ternary Weight Networks</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Fengfu Li
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Bin Liu
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Xiaoxing Wang
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Bo Zhang
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Junchi Yan
</span><span id="id1" class="ltx_note ltx_note_frontmatter ltx_thanks_correspondence ltx_role_thanks"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">thanks: </span>$†$: Equal contribution. <sup id="id1.1" class="ltx_sup">*</sup> Correspondence authors.</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">We present a memory and computation efficient ternary weight networks (TWNs) - with weights constrained to +1, 0 and -1. The Euclidian distance between full (float or double) precision weights and the ternary weights along with a scaling factor is minimized in training stage. Besides, a threshold-based ternary function is optimized to get an approximated solution which can be fast and easily computed. TWNs have shown better expressive abilities than binary precision counterparts. Meanwhile, TWNs achieve up to 16<math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> model compression rate and need fewer multiplications compared with the float32 precision counterparts. Extensive experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet datasets show that the TWNs achieve much better result than the Binary-Weight-Networks (BWNs) and the classification performance on MNIST and CIFAR-10 is very close to the full precision networks. We also verify our method on object detection task and show that TWNs significantly outperforms BWN by more than 10% mAP on PASCAL VOC dataset. The pytorch version of source code is available at: https://github.com/Thinklab-SJTU/twns.</p>
  
</div><span id="id2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_address"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">address: </span><sup id="id2.1" class="ltx_sup"><span id="id2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">1</span></sup>Institute of Applied Math., AMSS, CAS, Beijing, China
<br class="ltx_break">lifengfu12@mails.ucas.ac.cn, b.zhang@amt.ac.cn
<br class="ltx_break"><sup id="id2.2" class="ltx_sup"><span id="id2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">2</span></sup>MOE Key Lab of Artificial Intelligence, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China
<br class="ltx_break">{binliu_sjtu, figure1_wxx, yanjunchi}@sjtu.edu.cn</span></span></span>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction and Related Work</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Deep neural networks (DNN) have made significant improvements in lots of computer vision tasks such as object recognition <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite> and object detection <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>. This motivates interests to deploy the state-of-the-art DNN models to real world applications like smart phones, wearable embedded devices or other edge computing devices. However, these models often need considerable storage and computational power <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>, and can easily overburden the limited storage, battery power, and computer capabilities of the smart wearable embedded devices. As a result, it remains a challenge for the deployment.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To mitigate the storage and computational problem <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite>, methods that seek to binarize weights or activations in DNN models have been proposed. BinaryConnect <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite> uses a single sign function to binarize the weights. Binary Weight Networks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite> adopts the same binarization function but adds an extra scaling factor. The extensions of the previous methods are BinaryNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite> and XNOR-Net <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite> where both weights and activations are binary-valued. These models eliminate most of the multiplications in the forward and backward propagations, and thus own the potential of gaining significant benefits with specialized deep learning (DL) hardware by replacing many multiply-accumulate operations by simple accumulation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>. Besides, binary weight networks achieve up to 32<math id="S1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> model compression rate.
Despite the binary techniques, some other compression methods focus on identifying models with few parameters while preserving accuracy by compressing existing state-of-the-art DNN models in a lossy way. SqueezeNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite> is such a model that has 50<math id="S1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> fewer parameters than AlexNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite> but maintains AlexNet-level accuracy on ImageNet.
MobileNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite> and ShuffleNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite> propose lightweight architectures to reduce the parameters and computation cost. Other methods propose to search efficient architectures and achieves great performance on both classification <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite> and object detection <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>.
Deep Compression <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite> is another most recently proposed method that uses pruning, trained quantization and huffman coding for compressing neural networks. It reduced the storage requirement of AlexNet and VGG-16 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite> by 35<math id="S1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> and 49<math id="S1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively, without loss of accuracy. <span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">This paper has the following contributions:</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">1) To our best knowledge, this was the first (at least at its debut in arxiv) ternary weight quantization scheme to reduce storage and computational cost for deep neural networks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">2) We propose an approximated and universal solution with threshold-based ternary function for calculating the ternary weights of the raw neural networks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">3) Experiments show the efficacy of our approach on public benchmarks for both image classification and detection.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Ternary Weight Networks</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Advantage Overview</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We address the limited storage and computational resources issues by introducing ternary weight networks (TWNs), which constrain the weights to be ternary-valued: +1, 0 and -1. TWNs seek to make a balance between the full precision weight networks (FPWNs) counterparts and the binary precision weight networks (BPWNs) counterparts. The detailed features are listed as follows.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Expressive ability</span> In most recent network architectures such as VGG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>, GoogLeNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite> and ResNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>, a most commonly used convolutional filter is of size 3<math id="S2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>3. With binary precision, there is only <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2^{3\times 3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{3\times 3}</annotation></semantics></math> = 512 templates. However, a ternary filter with the same size owns <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3^{3\times 3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3^{3\times 3}</annotation></semantics></math> = 19683 templates, which gains 38<math id="S2.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> more stronger expressive abilities than the binary counterpart.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Model compression</span> In TWNs, 2-bit storage requirement is needed for a unit of weight. Thus, TWNs achieve up to 16<math id="S2.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> model compression rate compared with the float32 precision counterparts. Take VGG-19 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite> as an example, float version of the model needs <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>500M storage requirement, which can be reduced to <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>32M with ternary precision. Thus, although the compression rate of TWNs is 2<math id="S2.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> less than that of BPWNs, it is fair enough for compressing most of the existing state-of-the-art DNN models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Computational requirement</span> Compared with the BPWNs, TWNs own an extra zero state. However, the zero terms need not be accumulated for any multiple operations. Thus, the multiply-accumulate operations in TWNs keep unchanged compared with binary precision counterparts. As a result, it is also hardware-friendly for training large-scale networks with specialized DL hardware.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">In the following parts, we will give detailed descriptions about the ternary weight networks problem and an approximated but efficient solution. After that, a simple training algorithm with error back-propagation is introduced and the run time usage is described at last.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Problem Formulation</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To make the ternary weight networks perform well, we seek to minimize the Euclidian distance between the full precision weights <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐖</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}</annotation></semantics></math> and the ternary-valued weights <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\mathbf{W}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\mathbf{W}}</annotation></semantics></math> along with a nonnegative scaling factor <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>. The optimization problem is formulated as follows,</p>
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\left\{\begin{matrix}\alpha^{*},\tilde{\mathbf{{W}^{*}}}=\underset{\alpha,\tilde{\mathbf{W}}}{\arg\min}\quad\mathbf{J}(\alpha,\tilde{\mathbf{W}})=\left\|\mathbf{W-\alpha\tilde{\mathbf{W}}}\right\|_{2}^{2}\\
s.t.\quad\alpha\geq 0,\quad\tilde{\mathbf{W}_{i}}\in\left\{-1,0,+1\right\},i=1,2...,n\end{matrix}\right." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>{</mo><mtable displaystyle="true" accentunder="true"><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>min</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathsize="0.700em">α</mi><mo mathsize="0.700em">,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathsize="0.700em">𝐖</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></mrow></munder></mrow><mspace style="width:1.167em;" width="1.167em"></mspace><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐉</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo mathsize="0.700em">,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></mrow></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo><mspace style="width:1.167em;" width="1.167em"></mspace><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left\{\begin{matrix}\alpha^{*},\tilde{\mathbf{{W}^{*}}}=\underset{\alpha,\tilde{\mathbf{W}}}{\arg\min}\quad\mathbf{J}(\alpha,\tilde{\mathbf{W}})=\left\|\mathbf{W-\alpha\tilde{\mathbf{W}}}\right\|_{2}^{2}\\
s.t.\quad\alpha\geq 0,\quad\tilde{\mathbf{W}_{i}}\in\left\{-1,0,+1\right\},i=1,2...,n\end{matrix}\right.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Here <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathit{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathit{n}</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of the filter. With the approximation <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}\approx\alpha\tilde{\mathbf{W}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}\approx\alpha\tilde{\mathbf{W}}</annotation></semantics></math>, a basic block of forward propagation in ternary weight networks is as follows,</p>
<table id="S2.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\left\{\begin{matrix}\mathbf{Z}=\mathbf{X}\ast\mathbf{W}\approx\mathbf{X}\ast(\alpha\tilde{\mathbf{W}})=(\alpha\mathbf{X})\oplus\tilde{\mathbf{W}}\\
\mathbf{X}^{next}=\mathit{g}(\mathbf{Z})\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\end{matrix}\right." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>{</mo><mtable displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>𝐙</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>𝐗</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mi>𝐗</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐗</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>⊕</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>𝐗</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐙</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mspace style="width:13em;" width="13em"></mspace></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left\{\begin{matrix}\mathbf{Z}=\mathbf{X}\ast\mathbf{W}\approx\mathbf{X}\ast(\alpha\tilde{\mathbf{W}})=(\alpha\mathbf{X})\oplus\tilde{\mathbf{W}}\\
\mathbf{X}^{next}=\mathit{g}(\mathbf{Z})\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\end{matrix}\right.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{X}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐗</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{X}</annotation></semantics></math> is the input of the block; <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ast" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∗</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ast</annotation></semantics></math> is a convolution or inner product operation; <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathit{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathit{g}</annotation></semantics></math> is a nonlinear activation function; <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\oplus" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⊕</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\oplus</annotation></semantics></math> indicates a convolution or an inner product operation without multiplication; <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{Z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐙</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{Z}</annotation></semantics></math> is the output feature map of the neural network block. It can also be used as input of the next block.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Threshold-based Ternary Function</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">One way to solve the optimization Eq. <a href="#S2.E1" title="In 2.2 Problem Formulation ‣ 2 Ternary Weight Networks ‣ Ternary Weight Networks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> is to expand the cost function <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J(\alpha,\tilde{\mathbf{W}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J(\alpha,\tilde{\mathbf{W}})</annotation></semantics></math> and take the derivative w.r.t. <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\mathbf{W}_{i}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\mathbf{W}_{i}}</annotation></semantics></math> is respectively. However, this would get interdependent <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>α</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\mathbf{W}}_{i}^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>i</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\mathbf{W}}_{i}^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>. Thus, there is no deterministic solution in this way <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>. To overcome this, we try to find an approximated optimal solution with a threshold-based ternary function,</p>
<table id="S2.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\tilde{\mathbf{W}_{i}}=f(\mathbf{W}_{i}|\Delta)=\left\{\begin{matrix}+1&amp;\text{if}&amp;\mathbf{W}_{i}&gt;\Delta\\
0&amp;\text{if}&amp;\left|\mathbf{W}_{i}\right|\leq\Delta\\
-1&amp;\text{if}&amp;\mathbf{W}_{i}&lt;-\Delta\end{matrix}\right." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mtd><mtd><mtext>if</mtext></mtd><mtd><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd><mtext>if</mtext></mtd><mtd><mrow><mrow><mo>|</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>|</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mtd><mtd><mtext>if</mtext></mtd><mtd><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\mathbf{W}_{i}}=f(\mathbf{W}_{i}|\Delta)=\left\{\begin{matrix}+1&amp;\text{if}&amp;\mathbf{W}_{i}&gt;\Delta\\
0&amp;\text{if}&amp;\left|\mathbf{W}_{i}\right|\leq\Delta\\
-1&amp;\text{if}&amp;\mathbf{W}_{i}&lt;-\Delta\end{matrix}\right.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Here <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta</annotation></semantics></math> is an positive threshold parameter. With Eq. <a href="#S2.E3" title="In 2.3 Threshold-based Ternary Function ‣ 2 Ternary Weight Networks ‣ Ternary Weight Networks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, the original problem can be transformed to</p>
<table id="S2.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha^{*},\Delta^{*}=\underset{\alpha\geq 0,\Delta&gt;0}{\arg\min}(|\mathbf{W}_{\Delta}|\alpha^{2}-2(\sum_{i\in\mathbf{I}_{\Delta}}|\mathbf{W}_{i}|)\alpha+c_{\Delta})" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>α</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><munder accentunder="true"><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>min</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi mathsize="0.700em">α</mi><mo mathsize="0.700em">≥</mo><mn mathsize="0.700em">0</mn></mrow><mo mathsize="0.700em">,</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.700em" mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo mathsize="0.700em">&gt;</mo><mn mathsize="0.700em">0</mn></mrow></mrow></munder><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>α</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><munder><mo lspace="0em" movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>𝐈</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></msub></mrow></munder><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha^{*},\Delta^{*}=\underset{\alpha\geq 0,\Delta&gt;0}{\arg\min}(|\mathbf{W}_{\Delta}|\alpha^{2}-2(\sum_{i\in\mathbf{I}_{\Delta}}|\mathbf{W}_{i}|)\alpha+c_{\Delta})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{I}_{\Delta}=\left\{i{\Huge|}\left|\mathbf{W}_{i}\right|&gt;\Delta\right\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐈</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" mathsize="2.980em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>|</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>|</mo></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{I}_{\Delta}=\left\{i{\Huge|}\left|\mathbf{W}_{i}\right|&gt;\Delta\right\}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\mathbf{I}_{\Delta}|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>𝐈</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\mathbf{I}_{\Delta}|</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the number of elements in <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{I}_{\Delta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐈</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{I}_{\Delta}</annotation></semantics></math>; <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="c_{\Delta}={\textstyle\sum_{i\in\mathbf{I}_{\Delta}^{c}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mo>∑</mo><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐈</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>c</mi></msubsup></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{\Delta}={\textstyle\sum_{i\in\mathbf{I}_{\Delta}^{c}}}</annotation></semantics></math>; <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{i}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{i}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> is a <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> independent constant. Thus, for any given <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta</annotation></semantics></math>, the optimal <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> can be computed as follows,</p>
<table id="S2.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{\Delta}^{*}=\frac{1}{\left|\mathbf{I}_{\Delta}\right|}\sum_{i\in\mathbf{I}_{\Delta}}\left|\mathbf{W}_{i}\right|" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>α</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo>|</mo><msub><mi>𝐈</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></msub><mo>|</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>𝐈</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></msub></mrow></munder><mrow><mo>|</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>|</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha_{\Delta}^{*}=\frac{1}{\left|\mathbf{I}_{\Delta}\right|}\sum_{i\in\mathbf{I}_{\Delta}}\left|\mathbf{W}_{i}\right|</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.3" class="ltx_p">By substituting <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{\Delta}^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>α</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha_{\Delta}^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> into Eq. <a href="#S2.E4" title="In 2.3 Threshold-based Ternary Function ‣ 2 Ternary Weight Networks ‣ Ternary Weight Networks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, we get a <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta</annotation></semantics></math> dependent equation, which can be simplified as follows,</p>
<table id="S2.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta^{*}=\underset{\Delta&gt;0}{\arg\min}\frac{1}{\left|\mathbf{I}_{\Delta}\right|}(\sum_{i\in\mathbf{I}_{\Delta}}\left|\mathbf{W}_{i}\right|)^{2}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><munder accentunder="true"><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>min</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathsize="0.700em" mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo mathsize="0.700em">&gt;</mo><mn mathsize="0.700em">0</mn></mrow></munder><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo>|</mo><msub><mi>𝐈</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></msub><mo>|</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><munder><mo lspace="0em" movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>𝐈</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></msub></mrow></munder><mrow><mo>|</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>|</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta^{*}=\underset{\Delta&gt;0}{\arg\min}\frac{1}{\left|\mathbf{I}_{\Delta}\right|}(\sum_{i\in\mathbf{I}_{\Delta}}\left|\mathbf{W}_{i}\right|)^{2}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The above euqation has no straightforward solutions. Though discrete optimization can be made to solve the problem (due to states of <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is finite), it should be very time consuming. As a viable alternative, we make a single assumption that <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> are generated from uniform or normal distribution. In case of <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> are uniformly distributed in <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left[-\alpha,\alpha\right]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left[-\alpha,\alpha\right]</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta</annotation></semantics></math> lies in <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left(0,\alpha\right]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>α</mi><mo>]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left(0,\alpha\right]</annotation></semantics></math>, the approximated <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> is <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\alpha}{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mi>α</mi><mn>3</mn></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\alpha}{3}</annotation></semantics></math>, which equals to <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{2}{3}\mathbf{E}(\left|\mathbf{W}\right|)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐄</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo>|</mo><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>|</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{2}{3}\mathbf{E}(\left|\mathbf{W}\right|)</annotation></semantics></math>. When <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is generated from normal distributions <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N(0,\sigma^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N(0,\sigma^{2})</annotation></semantics></math>, the approximated <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> is 0.6<math id="S2.SS3.p3.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> which
equals to <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.75\mathbf{E}(\left|\mathbf{W}\right|)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.75</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐄</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo>|</mo><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>|</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.75\mathbf{E}(\left|\mathbf{W}\right|)</annotation></semantics></math>. Thus, we can use a rule of thumb that <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta^{*}\approx 0.75\mathbf{E}(\left|\mathbf{W}\right|)\approx\frac{0.75}{n}{\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}}\left|\mathbf{W}_{i}\right|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mn>0.75</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐄</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo>|</mo><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>|</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>0.75</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mrow><mo>|</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>|</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta^{*}\approx 0.75\mathbf{E}(\left|\mathbf{W}\right|)\approx\frac{0.75}{n}{\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}}\left|\mathbf{W}_{i}\right|</annotation></semantics></math> for simplicity.</p>
</div>
<figure id="algorithm1" class="ltx_float ltx_algorithm ltx_framed ltx_framed_top">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_float"><span id="algorithm1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Algorithm 1</span> </span>Train a M-layers CNN w/ ternary weights</figcaption>
<div id="algorithm1.4" class="ltx_listing ltx_lst_numbers_left ltx_framed ltx_framed_topbottom ltx_listing">
<div id="algorithm1.4.1" class="ltx_listingline">

<span id="algorithm1.4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Inputs :</span> A minibatch of inputs and targets (<math id="algorithm1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{I},\bm{Y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝑰</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝒀</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{I},\bm{Y}</annotation></semantics></math>), loss function <math id="algorithm1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L(\bm{Y},\hat{\bm{Y})}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>𝒀</mi><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">OPEN</mo><mi>𝒀</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em">CLOSE</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L(\bm{Y},\hat{\bm{Y})}</annotation></semantics></math> and current weight <math id="algorithm1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{W}^{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{W}^{t}</annotation></semantics></math>.
</div>
<div id="algorithm1.4.2" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="algorithm1.4.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hyper-parameter :</span> current learning rate <math id="algorithm1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta^{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>η</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta^{t}</annotation></semantics></math>.
</div>
<div id="algorithm1.4.3" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="algorithm1.4.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Outputs :</span> updated weight <math id="algorithm1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{W}^{t+1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{W}^{t+1}</annotation></semantics></math>, updated learning rate <math id="algorithm1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta^{t+1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>η</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta^{t+1}</annotation></semantics></math>.
</div>
<div id="algorithm1.4.4" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="algorithm1.4.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">1</span></span>
            Make the float32 weight filters as ternery ones:
</div>
<div id="algorithm1.4.5" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="algorithm1.4.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">2</span></span>
            <span id="algorithm1.4.5.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span> <em id="algorithm1.4.5.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic"><math id="algorithm1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m=~1~\text{to}~M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo rspace="0.608em">=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.330em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">to</mtext><mo lspace="0.330em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m=~1~\text{to}~M</annotation></semantics></math></em> <span id="algorithm1.4.5.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">do</span>
</div>
<div id="algorithm1.4.6" class="ltx_listingline"> <span class="ltx_rule" style="width:1px;height:100%;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span> 
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="algorithm1.4.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">3</span></span>
            <span id="algorithm1.4.6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span> <em id="algorithm1.4.6.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic"><math id="algorithm1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k^{th}\text{ filter in}~m^{th}~\text{layer}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>k</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic"> filter in</mtext><mo lspace="0.330em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>m</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">layer</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k^{th}\text{ filter in}~m^{th}~\text{layer}</annotation></semantics></math></em> <span id="algorithm1.4.6.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">do</span>
</div>
<div id="algorithm1.4.7" class="ltx_listingline"> <span class="ltx_rule" style="width:1px;height:100%;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span>  <span class="ltx_rule" style="width:1px;height:100%;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span> 
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="algorithm1.4.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">4</span></span>
            <math id="algorithm1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{mk}=\frac{0.75}{n}\|\mathcal{W}^{t}_{mk}\|_{l1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>0.75</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{mk}=\frac{0.75}{n}\|\mathcal{W}^{t}_{mk}\|_{l1}</annotation></semantics></math>
</div>
<div id="algorithm1.4.8" class="ltx_listingline"> <span class="ltx_rule" style="width:1px;height:100%;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span>  <span class="ltx_rule" style="width:1px;height:100%;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span> 
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="algorithm1.4.8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">5</span></span>
            <math id="algorithm1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\mathcal{W}}_{mk}={\text{\lx@text@lbrace-1, 0, +1\lx@text@rbrace}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>{-1, 0, +1}</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\mathcal{W}}_{mk}={\text{\lx@text@lbrace-1, 0, +1\lx@text@rbrace}}</annotation></semantics></math> , refer to Eq. <a href="#S2.E3" title="In 2.3 Threshold-based Ternary Function ‣ 2 Ternary Weight Networks ‣ Ternary Weight Networks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> 
</div>
<div id="algorithm1.4.9" class="ltx_listingline"> <span class="ltx_rule" style="width:1px;height:100%;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span>  <span class="ltx_rule" style="width:1px;height:100%;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span> 
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="algorithm1.4.9.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">6</span></span>
            <math id="algorithm1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{mk}=\frac{\mathcal{W}^{t}_{mk}\cdot\tilde{\mathcal{W}}_{mk}}{\tilde{\mathcal{W}}_{mk}\cdot\tilde{\mathcal{W}}_{mk}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha_{mk}=\frac{\mathcal{W}^{t}_{mk}\cdot\tilde{\mathcal{W}}_{mk}}{\tilde{\mathcal{W}}_{mk}\cdot\tilde{\mathcal{W}}_{mk}}</annotation></semantics></math> 
</div>
<div id="algorithm1.4.10" class="ltx_listingline"> <span class="ltx_rule" style="width:1px;height:100%;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span>  <span class="ltx_rule" style="width:1px;height:100%;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span> 
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="algorithm1.4.10.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">7</span></span>
            <math id="algorithm1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{T}_{mk}=\alpha_{mk}\tilde{\mathcal{W}}_{mk}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{T}_{mk}=\alpha_{mk}\tilde{\mathcal{W}}_{mk}</annotation></semantics></math>
</div>
<div id="algorithm1.4.11" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="algorithm1.4.11.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">8</span></span>
            <math id="algorithm1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\bm{Y}}=\text{{TernaryForward}}(\bm{I},\tilde{\mathcal{W}},\mathcal{\alpha})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>𝒀</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">TernaryForward</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑰</mi><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\bm{Y}}=\text{{TernaryForward}}(\bm{I},\tilde{\mathcal{W}},\mathcal{\alpha})</annotation></semantics></math> //<span id="algorithm1.4.11.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">standard forward propagation </span>
</div>
<div id="algorithm1.4.12" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="algorithm1.4.12.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">9</span></span>
            <math id="algorithm1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\partial L}{\partial\tilde{\mathcal{T}}}=\text{{TernaryBackward}}(\frac{\partial L}{\partial\hat{\bm{Y}}},\tilde{\mathcal{T}})" class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.900em">𝒯</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></mrow></mfrac><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" </div>
<div id="algorithm1.4.13" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="algorithm1.4.13.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">10</span></span>
            <math id="algorithm1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{W}^{t+1}=\text{{UpdateParameters}}(\mathcal{W}^{t},\frac{\partial L}{\partial\mathcal{T}},\eta_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.900em">𝒲</mi><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">t</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">+</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn></mrow></msup><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" mathsize="0.900em">UpdateParameters</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.900em">𝒲</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">t</mi></msup><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">∂</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">L</mi></mrow><mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">∂</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.900em">𝒯</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">η</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">t</mi></msub><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{W}^{t+1}=\text{{UpdateParameters}}(\mathcal{W}^{t},\frac{\partial L}{\partial\mathcal{T}},\eta_{t})</annotation></semantics></math><span id="algorithm1.4.13.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> // we use SGD in this paper </span>

</span>

</section>
<section id="S2.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.4 </span>Training of Ternary-Weight-Networks</h3>

<div id="S2.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">CNNs typically includes Convolution layer, Fully-Connected layer, Pooling layer (e.g.,Max-Pooling, Avg-Pooling), Batch-Normalization (BN) layer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite> and Activation layer (e.g.,ReLU, Sigmoid), in TWNs, we also follow the traditional neural network block design philosophy, the order of layers in a typical ternary block of TWNs is shown in Fig. <a href="#S2.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 2.4 Training of Ternary-Weight-Networks ‣ 2 Ternary Weight Networks ‣ Ternary Weight Networks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="1605.04711v3/imgs/twnsconvblock.jpg" id="S2.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:229/22;" width="229" height="22" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>A typical Ternary block in TWNs. In the forward pass, we apply ternarization operation for the weight of convolution layer meanwhile the float32 weight will be cached for future parameter update; in the backward pass, we calculate ternary weight gradient to update the float32 weight.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We borrow the parameter optimization strategy which successfully applied from BinaryConncet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite> and XNOR-Net <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>, in our design, ternarization only happens at the forward and backward pass in convolution and fully-connected layers, but in the parameters update stage, we still keep a copy of the full-precision parameters. In addition, two effective tricks, Batch-Normalization and learning rate step decay that drops the learning rate by a factor every few epochs, are adopted. We use stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with momentum to update the the parameters when training TWNs, the detailed training strategy show in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3 Experiments and Discussion ‣ Ternary Weight Networks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.5 </span>Inference of Ternary-Weight-Networks</h3>

<div id="S2.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the forward pass, the scaling factor <math id="S2.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> could be transformed to the inputs according to Eq. <a href="#S2.E2" title="In 2.2 Problem Formulation ‣ 2 Ternary Weight Networks ‣ Ternary Weight Networks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.
Thus, we only need to keep the ternary-valued weights and the scaling factors for deployment. This
would results up to 16<math id="S2.SS5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> model compression rate for deployment compared with the float32 precision counterparts.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F2" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<figure id="S2.F2.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center">
<div id="S2.F2.sf1.3" class="ltx_block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:103.5pt;"><img src="1605.04711v3/imgs/mnist.jpg" id="S2.F2.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:143/110;" width="143" height="110" alt="Refer to caption">
</div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F2.sf1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">(a)</span> </span><span id="S2.F2.sf1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">MNIST</span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S2.F2.sf2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center">
<div id="S2.F2.sf2.3" class="ltx_block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:103.5pt;"><img src="1605.04711v3/imgs/cifar10.jpg" id="S2.F2.sf2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:143/111;" width="143" height="111" alt="Refer to caption">
</div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F2.sf2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">(b)</span> </span><span id="S2.F2.sf2.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">CIFAR-10</span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">

</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Classification accuracy over training epochs MNIST (top-1 accuracy), CIFAR10 (top-1) and ImageNet (top-5).</figcaption>

</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Experiments and Discussion</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We benchmark Ternary Weight Networks (TWNs) with Binary Weight Networks (BPWNs) and Full Precision Networks (FPWNs) on both classification task (MNIST, CIFAR-10 and ImageNet) and object detection task (PASCAL VOC).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For a fair comparison, we keep the following configures to be same: network architecture, regularization method (L2 weight decay), learning rate scaling procedure (multi-step) and optimization method (SGD with momentum). BPWNs use sign function to binarize the weights and FPWNs use float-valued weights. See Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3 Experiments and Discussion ‣ Ternary Weight Networks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> for training configurations.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Backbones and hyperparameters setting for different datasets used by our method on three benchmarks.</figcaption>
<div id="S3.T1.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:338.1pt;height:39.5pt;vertical-align:-18.6pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-196.2pt,22.9pt) scale(0.462857268909146,0.462857268909146) ;">
<table id="S3.T1.2.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="S3.T1.2.1.1" class="ltx_tr">

</span></div>
</figure>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Experiments of Classification</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MNIST</span> is a collection of handwritten digits. It is a very popular dataset in the field of image processing. The LeNet-5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite> architecture we used in MNIST experiment is “32-C5 + MP2 + 64-C5 + MP2 + 512 FC + SVM” which starts with a 5x5 convolutional block that includes a convolution layer, a BN layer and a relu layer. Then a max-pooling layer is followed with stride 2. The “FC” is a fully connect block with 512 nodes. The top layer is a SVM classifier with 10 labels. Finally, hinge loss is minimized with SGD.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">CIFAR-10</span> consists of 10 classes with 6K color images of 32x32 resolution for each class. It is divided into 50K training and 10K testing images. We define a VGG inspired architecture, denoted as VGG-7, by “2<math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>(128-C3) + MP2 + 2<math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>(256-C3) + MP2 + 2<math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>(512-C3) + MP2 + 1024-FC + Softmax”. Compared with the architecture in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>, we ignore the last fully connected layer. We follow the data augmentation in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite> for training: 4 pixels are padded on each side, and a 32<math id="S3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>32 crop is randomly sampled from the padded image or its horizontal flip. At testing time, we only evaluate the single view of the original 32<math id="S3.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>32 image.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ImageNet</span> consists of about 1.2 million train images from 1000 categories and 50,000 validation images. ImageNet has higher resolution and greater diversity, is more close to real life than MNIST and CIFAR-10. We adopt the popular ResNet18 architecture <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite> as backbone. Besides, we also benchmark another enlarged counterpart whose number of filters in each block is 1.5<math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> of the original one which is termed as ResNet18B. In each training iteration, images are randomly cropped with 224<math id="S3.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>224 size. We do not use any resize tricks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite> or any color augmentation.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span>Classification accuracy (%) on ImageNet with ResNet18 (or ResNet18B in bracket) as backbones.</figcaption>

</figure>
<div id="S3.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S3.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 3.1 Experiments of Classification ‣ 3 Experiments and Discussion ‣ Ternary Weight Networks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows the classification results. On the small datasets (MNIST and CIFAR-10), TWNs achieve similar performance as FPWNs, while beats BPWNs. On the large-scale ImageNet dataset, BPWNs and TWNs both get poorer performance than FPWNs. However, the accuracy gap between TWNs and FPWNs is smaller than the gap between BPWNs and TWNs. In addition, when we change the backbone from ResNet18 to ResNet18B, as the model size is larger, the performance gap between TWNs (or BPWNs) and FPWNs has been reduced. This indicates low precision networks gain more merits from larger models than the full precision counterparts.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">The validation accuracy curves of different approaches across all training epochs on MNIST, CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets illustrate in Fig. <a href="#S2.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 2.5 Inference of Ternary-Weight-Networks ‣ 2 Ternary Weight Networks ‣ Ternary Weight Networks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. As we can see in the figure, obviously, BPWNs converge slowly and the training loss is not stable compared with TWNs and FPWNs. However, TWNs converge almost as fast and stably as FPWNs.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Experiments of Detection</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">PASCAL VOC</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite> consists of 20 classes with 11540 images and 27450 labeled objects. We adopt the popular YOLOv5 (small) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite> architecture and compare the performance of full precision, binary precision and ternary precision in Table <a href="#S3.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 3.1 Experiments of Classification ‣ 3 Experiments and Discussion ‣ Ternary Weight Networks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. Specifically, we initialize each model by the weights trained on MS-COCO dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite> (provided by YOLOv5) and fine-tune each model by 150 epochs. We observe that TWNs significantly outperforms BPWNs by more than 10% mAP, showing the great effectiveness of our method.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we have introduced the simple, efficient, and accurate ternary weight networks for real world AI application which can reduce the memory usage about 16x and the the computation about 2x. We present the optimization problem of TWNs and give an approximated solution with a simple but effective ternary function. The proposed TWNs achieve a balance between accuracy and model compression rate as well as potentially low computational requirements of BPWNs. Empirical results on public benchmarks show the superior performance of the proposed method.</p>
</div>
</section>

    <p><strong>Tip:</strong> You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.</p>
    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"
        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
